gap: No result ChatGPT got states how strong the signal is from a built-in preamp's LINE output. Fluance lists 140 mV (−17 dBV) for both the RT81 and the RT81+. That is about 7 dB below the −10 dBV (316 mV) consumer line level a powered speaker's AUX input is built for, so the shopper has to turn the volume up further than they would for a phone or CD player.
standout_why: I read three of the results ChatGPT got. valveandvinyl.com/turntables/crosley-alternatives gives the Audio-Technica decks '36 dB nominal gain' and calls the RT81 a 'true bypass', but it lists no output voltage for any deck. platterandplinth.com/turntables/best-with-preamp explains the PHONO/LINE switch and the double-RIAA problem of plugging LINE into a PHONO input. It also lists the Sony PS-LX3BT's −4/0/+6 dB gain select, but it gives no mV figure for any deck. fewbetter.com/best-turntable-with-built-in-phono-preamp no longer covers turntables at all (it lists kettles, backpacks and similar). ChatGPT's own answer already tells the shopper to set the switch to LINE, so that point is covered. The new information is the actual line-output level and how far it sits below consumer line level. vinylpickup.com could not be opened (TLS certificate error).
decides: This confirms rather than changes the pick. Both Fluance cards (RT81 at $299.99, RT81+ at $349.99) work with powered speakers or an AUX input on the LINE setting. However, 140 mV is a modest signal, so the speakers' volume will sit noticeably higher than with other sources. Fluance's full electronics bypass also means an external MM phono stage can replace the built-in one later. Shoppers whose speakers have weak AUX gain may prefer a deck with a higher rated line output. The Sony PS-LX3BT's +6 dB output gain step is built for that case, but I could not open a Sony or Audio-Technica page to put a maker number against the Fluance figure.
